subject: Mathematics

unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 6! In this unit you will explore three closely linked ideas: measurement of length, perimeter, and area. You will learn how to measure how long something is using the right units, how to find the distance all the way around a shape, and how to work out how much flat space a shape covers. These three skills belong together, and once you understand them you will start to see them everywhere in daily life.
learningPath: Preview the goals and core ideas
Learn methods and study worked examples
Complete guided practice, activities and games
Apply, explain and complete the Unit Challenge

provenance.transformation: Structured from the Cambridge Primary Mathematics 0096 — Stage 3 workbook source documents for screen presentation.

outcomes: Choose the best unit to measure a length: millimetres, centimetres, metres or kilometres.
Measure objects accurately using a ruler, lining up the zero mark correctly.
Convert between units in the metric system (mm ↔ cm ↔ m ↔ km).
Estimate a length sensibly and then measure to check.
Find the perimeter of rectangles, squares, triangles and other polygons.
Find the area of rectangles and squares using length × width.
Find area by counting squares on grid paper.
Explain the difference between perimeter and area, and use the correct units for each.

concepts.title: Length and Choosing the Right Unit
concepts.explanation:
Length is the measurement of how long something is from one end to the other. We measure length so often that we have several different units to choose from, depending on how big or small the thing is. Using the right unit is a bit like choosing the right container: you would not carry water in a spoon, and you would not fill a spoon from a bucket.

In the metric system – the system used almost everywhere in the world – the units of length from smallest to largest are:

Millimetre (mm) – for very small lengths, like the thickness of a coin or the width of a fingernail.

Centimetre (cm) – for small objects, like the length of a pencil, an eraser, or a book.

Metre (m) – for medium lengths, like the height of a door or the length of a room.

Kilometre (km) – for long distances, like the road from Mogadishu to the next town.

Choosing the right unit takes a little thought. Ask yourself: is this thing small, medium, or very large? If Farah wants to measure her pencil, centimetres are perfect – the pencil is about 15 cm. If she used kilometres, the answer would be a tiny fraction that is hard to picture. If she wants to measure the length of the football pitch at Nuur Academy, metres are best. And if she wants to describe the distance from Hargeisa to Berbera, only kilometres make sense.
concepts.example: Here is a helpful way to picture the sizes. A millimetre is about the thickness of a coin. Ten of those millimetres side by side make one centimetre – about the width of your smallest fingernail. One hundred of those centimetres make one metre – about the length of a big step or the height of a young child. And one thousand of those metres make one kilometre – a distance you might walk in about ten or fifteen minutes. When you can picture each unit in your mind, choosing the right one becomes easy.

concepts.title: Measuring with a Ruler
concepts.explanation:
A ruler is a tool for measuring length. Most rulers show centimetres, with each centimetre divided into ten small parts – those small parts are millimetres. Measuring well is a skill, and doing it carefully makes all the difference between a right answer and a wrong one.

Follow these three steps every time you measure with a ruler:

Place the zero mark of the ruler exactly at one end of the object. This is the most important step – do not start at the edge of the ruler or at the number 1 by mistake.

Look along the ruler to the other end of the object and read the number there.

Look straight down at the ruler, not from the side. Reading from an angle makes the measurement wrong. This mistake is called a parallax error.

Let us imagine Hassan measuring a leaf. He lines up the zero mark of his ruler with the bottom tip of the leaf. He looks straight down and sees that the top tip of the leaf reaches the mark halfway between 8 cm and 9 cm. So the leaf is about 8 cm and 5 mm, which we can also write as 8.5 cm. Notice that Hassan did not need the measurement to be a whole number – real objects are often between the marks.
concepts.example: A common slip is to start measuring from the number 1 instead of from 0. If you do that, every measurement is 1 cm too big. Another slip is to let the ruler drift so the zero mark is not quite at the end of the object. Always check that the zero mark is lined up before you read the other end. Careful placement now saves you from wrong answers later.

concepts.title: Converting Between Units
concepts.explanation:
Here are the key metric conversions to learn by heart:

10 millimetres (mm) = 1 centimetre (cm)

100 centimetres (cm) = 1 metre (m)

1000 metres (m) = 1 kilometre (km)

There is a simple pattern to converting. When you go from a larger unit to a smaller unit, the number gets bigger, so you multiply. When you go from a smaller unit to a larger unit, the number gets smaller, so you divide. This makes sense: it takes many small units to make up one big unit, so there will always be more small units.

Let us work through some examples. To change 5 m into centimetres, we are going from a larger unit (m) to a smaller unit (cm), so we multiply by 100: 5 × 100 = 500 cm. To change 250 cm into metres, we are going from a smaller unit to a larger unit, so we divide by 100: 250 ÷ 100 = 2.5 m. To change 3 km into metres, we multiply by 1000: 3 × 1000 = 3000 m. And to change 15 mm into centimetres, we divide by 10: 15 ÷ 10 = 1.5 cm.
concepts.example: Some measurements are given in two units at once, like 2 m 35 cm. To turn this into a single unit, change the larger part into the smaller unit and add. So 2 m 35 cm becomes 200 cm + 35 cm = 235 cm. Going the other way, 450 cm can be split into 4 whole metres (400 cm) with 50 cm left over, so 450 cm = 4 m 50 cm. Being able to move smoothly between units is one of the most useful measurement skills you can have.

concepts.title: Estimating Length
concepts.explanation:
An estimate is a sensible guess about a measurement made before you measure exactly. Estimating is useful when you do not need an exact answer, and it is also a way of checking – if your careful measurement is far from your estimate, that is a warning to measure again. Good mathematicians estimate first out of habit.

To make a good estimate, think about the size of the unit and compare the object to something you already know. You know your hand is about 7 cm wide, so you can use it as a ruler in your mind. You know a big step is about 1 m, so you can pace out a room to estimate its length. When Idris wants to estimate the length of his desk, he pictures how many hand-widths would fit along it, then turns that into centimetres.
concepts.example: Here are some useful lengths to keep in your memory as reference points: a pencil is about 15–20 cm long, a door is about 2 m tall, a new pencil eraser is about 4 cm long, and a doorway is about 1 m wide. When you carry a few known lengths in your head, every estimate becomes more accurate. Estimating and measuring work together like two hands – one guesses, the other checks.

concepts.title: Perimeter – the Distance Around
concepts.explanation:
Perimeter is the distance all the way around the outside of a shape. Imagine an ant walking around the very edge of a shape until it returns to where it started – the total distance it walks is the perimeter. Because perimeter is a length, it is measured in units of length like millimetres, centimetres, or metres. It is never measured in square units.

The most basic way to find a perimeter is simply to add up the lengths of all the sides. This works for any shape with straight sides. For example, if a rectangle has sides of 5 cm, 8 cm, 5 cm, and 8 cm, its perimeter is 5 + 8 + 5 + 8 = 26 cm. If a triangle has sides of 5 cm, 7 cm, and 9 cm, its perimeter is 5 + 7 + 9 = 21 cm.

For rectangles and squares there are helpful shortcuts, because their sides follow a rule. In a rectangle, the opposite sides are equal, so there are really only two different side lengths: the length and the width. Instead of adding four numbers, we can add the length and width and then double the answer:

Perimeter of a rectangle = 2 × (length + width).

For the rectangle above with length 8 cm and width 5 cm: Perimeter = 2 × (8 + 5) = 2 × 13 = 26 cm. Notice this matches the answer we got by adding all four sides – the formula is just a faster way to do the same thing.

In a square, all four sides are exactly the same length, so we can multiply one side by four:

Perimeter of a square = 4 × side length.
concepts.example: So a square with sides of 6 cm has a perimeter of 4 × 6 = 24 cm. For any other polygon – a pentagon, a hexagon, or an irregular shape – there is no special shortcut, so you simply measure every side and add them all together. Perimeter is used whenever we need to know how far it is around something: how much fencing a garden needs, how much ribbon goes around a gift, or how much trim borders a picture frame.

concepts.title: Area – the Space Inside
concepts.explanation:
Area is the amount of flat space inside a shape. If perimeter is the distance an ant walks around the edge, then area is the amount of floor the ant could cover with tiles inside the shape. Because area measures a flat surface, it is measured in square units, such as square centimetres (cm²) or square metres (m²).

The best way to understand area is to think of covering the shape with unit squares. A square centimetre (cm²) is a little square that is exactly 1 cm long on each side. The area of a shape is simply the number of these unit squares that fit inside it. If a rectangle can be covered by 40 of these 1 cm squares with no gaps and no overlaps, then its area is 40 cm².

Imagine a rectangle that is 8 cm long and 5 cm wide, drawn on grid paper. Along the length you can fit 8 squares in a row. There are 5 such rows going down. So the total number of squares is 8 in each row, 5 rows, which is 8 × 5 = 40 squares. This is exactly why the rule for the area of a rectangle is:

Area of a rectangle = length × width.
concepts.example: So for our rectangle, Area = 8 cm × 5 cm = 40 cm². The little ² (the raised 2, said “squared”) tells us we are measuring area, not length. A square is just a special rectangle where the length and width are equal, so: Area of a square = side × side.

methods.title: How to measure with a ruler
methods.example: Which unit — mm, cm, m, or km — is best for measuring the distance between two cities?
steps: Line up the zero mark with one end of the object.
Read the number at the other end of the object.
Look straight down to avoid a reading error.

methods.title: How to find a perimeter
methods.example: A ribbon is 2 m 35 cm long. How long is it in centimetres?
steps: Find the length of every side.
Add all the side lengths together (or use the rectangle or square formula).
Write the answer in a length unit such as cm or m.

methods.title: How to find an area
methods.example: A rectangular garden near Kismaayo has a length of 8 m and a width of 5 m. How much fencing is needed to go around it?
steps: Find the length and the width.
Multiply length by width.
Write the answer in square units such as cm² or m².

methods.title: How to convert units
methods.example: A square picture frame has sides of 15 cm each. What is the distance around the frame?
steps: Decide if you are going to a smaller or larger unit.
Smaller unit: multiply (×10, ×100 or ×1000).
Larger unit: divide (÷10, ÷100 or ÷1000).

methods.title: Area of a rectangle
methods.example: A rectangular carpet is 6 m long and 4 m wide. What is its area?
steps: Area asks how much flat space the carpet covers, so we multiply: Area = length × width = 6 × 4 = 24 m².
Do not forget the square units — area is always in square units.
Check by swapping the order: 4 × 6 should give the same answer, 24 m².

methods.title: Area of a square
methods.example: A square tile has sides of 20 cm. What is the area of the tile?
steps: Area of a square = side × side = 20 × 20 = 400 cm².
Remember a square's four sides are all equal, so you only need one measurement.
Check by re-multiplying 20 × 20 to confirm 400 cm².

workedExamples.title: Choose the right unit
workedExamples.prompt: Which unit — mm, cm, m, or km — is best for measuring the distance between two cities?
workedExamples.solution: Cities are very far apart, so we need the largest unit of length. The best unit is the kilometre (km). Millimetres or centimetres would give a huge, awkward number, and even metres would be in the thousands.

workedExamples.title: Convert metres to centimetres
workedExamples.prompt: A ribbon is 2 m 35 cm long. How long is it in centimetres?
workedExamples.solution: First change the metres into centimetres: 2 m = 2 × 100 = 200 cm. Then add the extra centimetres: 200 + 35 = 235 cm. When you go from a larger unit to a smaller unit, the number gets bigger, which matches what we found.

workedExamples.title: Perimeter of a rectangle
workedExamples.prompt: A rectangular garden near Kismaayo has a length of 8 m and a width of 5 m. How much fencing is needed to go around it?
workedExamples.solution: Fencing goes around the edge, so we need the perimeter. Using the formula: Perimeter = 2 × (length + width) = 2 × (8 + 5) = 2 × 13 = 26 m of fencing. We could also add all four sides: 8 + 5 + 8 + 5 = 26 m, which gives the same answer.

workedExamples.title: Perimeter of a square
workedExamples.prompt: A square picture frame has sides of 15 cm each. What is the distance around the frame?
workedExamples.solution: All four sides of a square are equal, so Perimeter = 4 × side = 4 × 15 = 60 cm.

workedExamples.title: Area of a rectangle
workedExamples.prompt: A rectangular carpet is 6 m long and 4 m wide. What is its area?
workedExamples.solution: Area asks how much flat space the carpet covers, so we multiply: Area = length × width = 6 × 4 = 24 m². Do not forget the square units — area is always in square units.

workedExamples.title: Area of a square
workedExamples.prompt: A square tile has sides of 20 cm. What is the area of the tile?
workedExamples.solution: Area of a square = side × side = 20 × 20 = 400 cm².

workedExamples.title: Find a missing side
workedExamples.prompt: A rectangle has a perimeter of 30 cm. Its length is 8 cm. What is its width?
workedExamples.solution: Start from the formula: Perimeter = 2 × (length + width). So 30 = 2 × (8 + width). Divide both sides by 2: 15 = 8 + width. Take away 8: width = 15 − 8 = 7 cm. You can check: 2 × (8 + 7) = 2 × 15 = 30 cm. Correct!

workedExamples.title: Perimeter and area together
workedExamples.prompt: A rectangular room is 6 m long and 4 m wide. How much skirting board is needed to go around it, and how many square tiles of 1 m² are needed to cover the floor?
workedExamples.solution: Baseboard goes around the edge, so use perimeter: 2 × (6 + 4) = 2 × 10 = 20 m of baseboard. Tiles cover the floor, so use area: 6 × 4 = 24 m², which means 24 tiles. Notice how one question needed perimeter and the other needed area — always ask which you need.

workedExamples.title: Tiles to cover a floor
workedExamples.prompt: A rectangular room is 6 m long and 5 m wide. Each square tile has an area of 1 m². How many tiles cover the floor?
workedExamples.solution: Find the floor area: 6 × 5 = 30 m². Since each tile covers 1 m², you need 30 ÷ 1 = 30 tiles.

workedExamples.title: Same area, different perimeter
workedExamples.prompt: Find two different rectangles with whole-number sides that each have an area of 12 cm². Which has the smaller perimeter?
workedExamples.solution: We need pairs of whole numbers that multiply to 12. One choice is 1 × 12, another is 3 × 4. Both give an area of 12 cm². Their perimeters differ: the 1 by 12 rectangle has perimeter 2 × (1 + 12) = 26 cm, while the 3 by 4 rectangle has perimeter 2 × (3 + 4) = 14 cm. So the 3 by 4 rectangle has the smaller perimeter. Shapes closer to a square use less perimeter for the same area.

workedExamples.title: For a rectangle 9 m long and 5 m wide, find both the…
workedExamples.prompt: For a rectangle 9 m long and 5 m wide, find both the perimeter and the area.

workedExamples.title: Find all the rectangles with whole-number sides that…
workedExamples.prompt: Find all the rectangles with whole-number sides that have a perimeter of 20 cm. List each length and width.
workedExamples.solution: Perimeter 20 cm means length + width = 10: so 1×9, 2×8, 3×7, 4×6, and 5×5.

activities.title: Measurement Scavenger Hunt
activities.materials: a ruler or tape measure, paper, a pencil.
steps: Make a list of 10 objects around your home.
Estimate the length of each object first, and write your guess down.
Measure each object with your ruler or tape measure and write the real length.
Compare your estimates with the real measurements. Which were closest?
For each object, decide whether centimetres or metres is the better unit.

activities.title: Perimeter Walk
activities.materials: a tape measure or a length of string, paper, a pencil.
steps: Choose a rectangular object or space – a table, a mat, or even a room.
Measure each side and write down the length.
Add all the sides together to find the perimeter.
Check your answer using the rectangle formula: 2 × (length + width).
Do the same for three more objects and compare their perimeters.

activities.title: Area with Square Tiles
activities.materials: grid paper, or small square objects like biscuits, tiles, or paper squares.
steps: Draw a rectangle on grid paper, or lay out a rectangle using square objects.
Count the squares inside to find the area.
Now find the area using length × width and check that the two answers match.
Make three more rectangles and record the length, width, and area of each.
Challenge: Make a shape on grid paper that has an area of 16 squares but is not a rectangle. Count the squares to prove it.

activities.title: Same Perimeter, Different Area (Investigation)
activities.materials: grid paper, a ruler, a pencil.
steps: On grid paper, draw four different rectangles that all have a perimeter of 24 cm.
Estimate the area of each rectangle before counting.
Count the squares to find the exact area of each.
Record your results in a table with columns for length, width, perimeter, and area.
Which rectangle has the largest area? What do you notice about its shape?

activities.title: Design a Garden (Family Task)
activities.materials: paper, a pencil, and a family member to work with.
steps: Imagine you are planning a rectangular vegetable garden for your family near Hargeisa.
Choose a length and a width in metres and draw the garden.
Work out the perimeter to decide how much fencing wire is needed.
Work out the area to decide how much space there is for planting.
Talk with your family member about whether a long thin garden or a square one is better, and why.

activities.title: The Conversion Card Game
steps: On some cards write measurements in one unit, like 3 m, 40 mm, or 2 km.
On other cards write the matching measurement in a different unit, like 300 cm, 4 cm, or 2000 m.
Shuffle the cards and lay them face down.
Take turns turning over two cards and keep the pair if they are equal. The player with the most pairs wins.
This game makes converting between units quick and automatic.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Find all the rectangles with whole-number sides that have a perimeter of 20 cm. List each length and width.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Perimeter 20 cm means length + width = 10: so 1×9, 2×8, 3×7, 4×6, and 5×5.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Find all the rectangles with whole-number sides that have an area of 36 cm². Which one has the smallest perimeter?
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Area 36 cm² gives 1×36, 2×18, 3×12, 4×9, and 6×6; the 6×6 square has the smallest perimeter (24 cm).

reasoningPrompts.prompt: A triangle has a perimeter of 24 cm. Two of its sides are 8 cm and 9 cm. Find the third side.
A rectangle has a width of 5 cm and a length that is twice its width. Find its perimeter and its area.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Length = 2 × 5 = 10 cm; Perimeter = 2 × (10 + 5) = 2 × 15 = 30 cm; Area = 10 × 5 = 50 cm².

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Draw (or imagine) two different shapes that both have an area of 16 cm² but different perimeters. Explain how this is possible.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: A 4 cm × 4 cm square has area 16 cm² (4 × 4 = 16) and perimeter 16 cm. A 2 cm × 8 cm rectangle also has area 16 cm² (2 × 8 = 16) but perimeter 2 × (2 + 8) = 20 cm. The areas match because both give 16 square units, but the perimeters differ because the shapes are different — a long thin rectangle has more perimeter than a square with the same area.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Area – the Space Inside.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Area is the amount of flat space inside a shape. If perimeter is the distance an ant walks around the edge, then area is the amount of floor the ant could cover with tiles inside the shape. Because area measures a flat surface, it is measured in square units, such as square centimetres (cm²) or square metres (m²). The best way to understand area is to think of covering the shape with unit squares. A square centimetre (cm²) is a little square that is exactly 1 cm long on each side. The area of a shape is simply the total number of unit squares needed to cover it completely, with no gaps and no overlaps.

selfAssessment: I can choose the best unit to measure a length: millimetres, centimetres, metres or kilometres.
I can measure objects accurately using a ruler, lining up the zero mark correctly.
I can convert between units in the metric system (mm ↔ cm ↔ m ↔ km).
I can estimate a length sensibly and then measure to check.
I can find the perimeter of rectangles, squares, triangles and other polygons.
I can find the area of rectangles and squares using length × width.
I can find area by counting squares on grid paper.
I can explain the difference between perimeter and area, and use the correct units for each.
